title: Aleph Track — First Beginning
description: A 36-lesson first Hebrew sequence for right-to-left direction, letter recognition, vowel cues, familiar words, and confidence before Bet. The order groups useful visual and sound families instead of following strict alphabet order.

lessons.title: Opening the Hebrew Doorway
lessons.focus: Begin at the right; move toward the left.
lessons.goal: Start Hebrew at the right edge and move toward the left.
teach: Start Hebrew at the right edge and move toward the left.
Keep the page upright. Touch the right edge to find the start, then trace toward the left.
examples: The start belongs at the right edge.
Move toward the finish at the left edge.
practice: Place a start mark at the right edge; trace a path toward the left.
Take turns pointing to the Hebrew start and saying the direction aloud.
lessons.check: Start Hebrew at the right edge and move toward the left.
lessons.question: Where do Hebrew readers begin?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Start Hebrew at the right edge and move toward the left.

lessons.title: Hebrew Letters Are Not English Letters
lessons.goal: Recognize that Hebrew has its own letter shapes and names.
teach: Recognize that Hebrew has its own letter shapes and names.
Compare a Hebrew letter with a Latin letter. Name the script first, then identify the Hebrew shapes.
practice: Sort Hebrew letters and Latin letters into separate groups.
Choose one Hebrew letter; point to it and say its name after a teacher model.
lessons.check: Recognize that Hebrew has its own letter shapes and names.
lessons.question: Which is a Hebrew letter?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize that Hebrew has its own letter shapes and names.

lessons.title: The Hebrew Side of the Page
lessons.goal: Track a Hebrew line from right to left, one word at a time.
teach: Track a Hebrew line from right to left, one word at a time.
Track one short line with a finger. Pause at each space and restart from the right side of the next word.
examples: Start with Aleph on the right. Continue left to Bet, then Gimel.
practice: Track a whole line from right to left with your finger.
Pause at the space between words, then continue from the next word on the right.
lessons.check: Track a Hebrew line from right to left, one word at a time.
lessons.question: Which way do you follow a Hebrew line?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Track a Hebrew line from right to left, one word at a time.

lessons.title: Aleph: The First Silent Carrier
lessons.goal: Aleph carries a vowel mark in these examples; hear the modeled ahhh sound without adding an Aleph consonant.
teach: Aleph does not add a consonant sound in these examples; it carries the vowel.
Patach is the Stick Vowel and Qamatz the Stick with a Handle. Point below the letter; both say ahhh in today’s examples.
practice: Circle Patach and box Qamatz.
Point to א then the mark below; say ahhh for אַ and אָ.
lessons.check: Point to Aleph and its vowel mark, then say the modeled ahhh sound.
lessons.question: What should you notice when reading these Aleph examples?
options: The vowel mark supplies the modeled sound
Aleph adds an English A sound
The vowel mark is part of the picture
lessons.teacher_note: Model the Stick Vowel patach and Stick with Handle qamatz with an ahhh sound for these examples. The cue names are memory aids, not formal vowel definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. The vowel mark supplies the modeled sound carried by Aleph.

lessons.title: Ayin: Another Silent Carrier
lessons.goal: Ayin is a distinct letter; use a gentle class pronunciation and respect tradition differences.
teach: Ayin is not Aleph; it is a separate letter with its own name.
Ayin has different pronunciations in Hebrew traditions. Use the class model and describe variation respectfully.
practice: Match עַ and עָ to the two ahhh marks.
Practice the teacher’s pronunciation model and listen respectfully to other traditions.
lessons.check: Ayin is a distinct letter; use a gentle class pronunciation and respect tradition differences.
lessons.question: How should learners handle pronunciation differences?
options: Use a clear model and respect established traditions
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Ayin is a distinct letter; use a gentle class pronunciation and respect tradition differences.

lessons.title: Silent Carriers Review: Aleph and Ayin
lessons.goal: Recognize Aleph and Ayin, then pair them with the two ahhh marks.
teach: Recognize Aleph and Ayin, then pair them with the two ahhh marks.
Place א and ע cards in separate groups. Say each name before matching it to its vowel example.
practice: Sort Aleph and Ayin letter cards.
Pair each letter with a Stick Vowel and explain which part gives the sound.
lessons.check: Recognize Aleph and Ayin, then pair them with the two ahhh marks.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Silent Carriers Review: Aleph and Ayin”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Aleph and Ayin, then pair them with the two ahhh marks.

lessons.title: Bet and Vet: The Dot Matters
lessons.goal: Distinguish Bet’s inside dot from Vet’s open center; learn the Pea Vowel beneath the letter.
teach: Bet has a dot inside—the ball—and Vet has an open center—the void.
The Pea Vowel is one dot beneath a letter and says eee. The dot inside Bet and the dot below it do different jobs.
practice: Circle the Bet ball and underline the Pea below.
Read בִּ and בִ after naming the inside dot and the beneath dot.
lessons.check: Distinguish Bet’s inside dot from Vet’s open center; learn the Pea Vowel beneath the letter.
lessons.question: Where is the Pea Vowel?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Distinguish Bet’s inside dot from Vet’s open center; learn the Pea Vowel beneath the letter.

lessons.title: Dagesh Practice: Seeing Before Saying
lessons.goal: Notice the dagesh dot inside a letter before saying its modeled consonant sound.
teach: Dagesh is the dot inside a letter. For Bet and Kaf in these beginner examples, it helps identify the firmer sound.
Always point to the letter and the inside dot before trying its teacher-modeled sound.
practice: Find which examples have a dot inside.
Compare בּ/ב and כּ/כ; echo the community sound model.
lessons.check: Notice the dagesh dot inside a letter before saying its modeled consonant sound.
lessons.question: What should you inspect before choosing a modeled sound?
options: The letter and its inside dot
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Notice the dagesh dot inside a letter before saying its modeled consonant sound.

lessons.title: Bet in Simple Words and Names
lessons.goal: Read two Bet examples that use the previously taught ahhh marks.
teach: Only use marks already introduced: Patach and Qamatz.
Point to the letters from the right, blend each known part, then say the word.
practice: Cover the meanings and read בַּת and בָּא from right to left.
Uncover the gloss; tell which word means daughter and which means came.
lessons.check: Read two Bet examples that use the previously taught ahhh marks.
lessons.question: Which word means daughter?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Read two Bet examples that use the previously taught ahhh marks.

lessons.title: Mem and Final Mem: A Letter with an Ending Form
lessons.goal: Recognize Mem in its regular form and its final form at a word’s end.
teach: Mem says m in both forms. Final Mem ם is used at the end of a word.
Do not call ם a new letter; it is Mem’s ending shape.
practice: Match מ with ם and find each in a letter row.
Place ם only in the ending box.
lessons.check: Recognize Mem in its regular form and its final form at a word’s end.
lessons.question: Where does Final Mem appear?
options: At the end of a word
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Mem in its regular form and its final form at a word’s end.

lessons.title: Shin and Sin: The Dot’s Place Matters
lessons.goal: The right-side dot cues Shin; the left-side dot cues Sin.
teach: Shin and Sin share a letter body. The dot’s side changes the reading.
Right-side dot: Shin, sh. Left-side dot: Sin, s. Follow the classroom model.
practice: Mark the side of each dot before naming Shin or Sin.
Sort the sh and s forms; read only after checking the dot.
lessons.check: The right-side dot cues Shin; the left-side dot cues Sin.
lessons.question: Which dot position cues Shin, sh?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. The right-side dot cues Shin; the left-side dot cues Sin.

lessons.title: Lamed: The Tall Letter
lessons.goal: Recognize Lamed by its tall stroke and blend it with known ahhh vowels.
teach: Recognize Lamed by its tall stroke and blend it with known ahhh vowels.
Compare ל with nearby short letters. Its tall stroke rises above the usual letter height.
practice: Find Lamed among short letters.
Trace ל, then blend לַ and לָ.
lessons.check: Recognize Lamed by its tall stroke and blend it with known ahhh vowels.
lessons.question: Which is the tall letter?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Lamed by its tall stroke and blend it with known ahhh vowels.

lessons.title: The Dot Over and Vav-Cholam: Oh
lessons.goal: Cholam is the dot over a letter; Vav-Cholam carries the oh sound.
teach: The Cholam dot above a letter cues oh: “Over says Ohhhver Oh.”
When the dot is above Vav, Vav-Cholam carries oh. Point to the mark before reading.
practice: Point to the dot over the letter in בֹּ and name oh.
Find the dot over Vav in בוֹ and compare the two oh patterns.
lessons.check: Cholam is the dot over a letter; Vav-Cholam carries the oh sound.
lessons.question: What sound does the Cholam dot cue here?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Cholam is the dot over a letter; Vav-Cholam carries the oh sound.

lessons.title: Vav: The Connecting Letter
lessons.goal: Recognize Vav in its upright shape and in a familiar vowel pattern.
teach: Recognize Vav in its upright shape and in a familiar vowel pattern.
Compare ו with ל: both rise, but Vav is shorter. Find the dot in וֹ and recall its oh sound.
practice: Find Vav in a mixed letter row.
Compare ו with י; name which one is taller.
lessons.check: Recognize Vav in its upright shape and in a familiar vowel pattern.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Vav: The Connecting Letter”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Vav in its upright shape and in a familiar vowel pattern.

lessons.title: Yod: Small but Important
lessons.goal: Recognize Yod as a small but important letter.
teach: Recognize Yod as a small but important letter.
Find י beside taller letters. Notice how small it is, then locate it again in a word.
practice: Find Yod without relying on its place in a row.
Trace י and blend יַ using the already taught Patach.
lessons.check: Recognize Yod as a small but important letter.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Yod: Small but Important”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Yod as a small but important letter.

lessons.title: Hey: A Letter with Breath
lessons.goal: Recognize Hey by its open shape and gentle breath sound.
teach: Recognize Hey by its open shape and gentle breath sound.
Look for the open space in ה. Say the name, then echo the gentle breath sound modeled by the teacher.
practice: Point to the opening in Hey.
Compare ה and ח; use the class sound model for each.
lessons.check: Recognize Hey by its open shape and gentle breath sound.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Hey: A Letter with Breath”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Hey by its open shape and gentle breath sound.

lessons.title: Name-Building Review and the Three Eggs
lessons.goal: Recognize Yod, Vav, and Hey; introduce Segol, the Three Eggs eh vowel.
teach: Yod, Vav, and Hey have distinct sizes and openings.
Segol is three dots beneath a letter: three eggs cue eh. Say the vowel after naming the letter and the mark.
practice: Compare Yod, Vav, and Hey by size and opening.
Count the three Segol dots; read בֶּ and מֶ as eh.
lessons.check: Recognize Yod, Vav, and Hey; introduce Segol, the Three Eggs eh vowel.
lessons.question: How many dots make the Three Eggs vowel?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Yod, Vav, and Hey; introduce Segol, the Three Eggs eh vowel.

lessons.title: Dalet and Resh: Careful Corners
lessons.goal: Compare Dalet and Resh by their small corner and stroke differences.
teach: Compare Dalet and Resh by their small corner and stroke differences.
Set ד and ר side by side. Follow the upper corner and right edge to tell the shapes apart.
practice: Place ד and ר side by side.
Trace the corner detail slowly; identify each letter in a mixed row.
lessons.check: Compare Dalet and Resh by their small corner and stroke differences.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Dalet and Resh: Careful Corners”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Compare Dalet and Resh by their small corner and stroke differences.

lessons.title: Kaf, Khaf, and Final Kaf
lessons.goal: Distinguish Kaf, Khaf, and final Kaf; the dot and final position matter.
teach: Distinguish Kaf, Khaf, and final Kaf; the dot and final position matter.
The regular Kaf כּ and Khaf כ share a family shape; the dot marks the firmer sound in this beginner comparison. Final Kaf ך is used only at a word’s end.
practice: Sort כּ, כ, and ך by dot and word position.
Keep the final form in the ending box and echo the Khaf model.
lessons.check: Distinguish Kaf, Khaf, and final Kaf; the dot and final position matter.
lessons.question: Which is Final Kaf?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Distinguish Kaf, Khaf, and final Kaf; the dot and final position matter.

lessons.title: Final Forms Family I: Mem, Nun, Kaf
lessons.focus: מ ם נ ן כ ך
lessons.goal: Match Mem, Nun, and Kaf with their final forms.
teach: Mem, Nun, and Kaf each change shape at a word’s end.
Regular and final forms keep their letter identity and sound; use the final shape only at the end.
practice: Match each middle form with its final partner.
Write one family pair and explain where the ending shape belongs.
lessons.check: Match Mem, Nun, and Kaf with their final forms.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Final Forms Family I: Mem, Nun, Kaf”?
options: מ ם נ ן כ ך
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Match Mem, Nun, and Kaf with their final forms.

lessons.title: Final Forms Family II: Pey and Tsadi
lessons.goal: Match Peh and Tsadi with their final forms.
teach: Peh and Tsadi also change shape at the end of a word.
Match פ with ף and צ with ץ before reading any example.
practice: Match פ/ף and צ/ץ.
Sort regular and final forms, then read the letter names.
lessons.check: Match Peh and Tsadi with their final forms.
lessons.question: Which is Final Tsadi?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Match Peh and Tsadi with their final forms.

lessons.title: Final Forms Review: The Ending Doorway
lessons.goal: Review all five final letter shapes and place each at a word’s end.
teach: There are five common final forms: ך ם ן ף ץ.
Their shapes change at a word’s end; the reading direction does not.
practice: Place all five final forms in ending boxes.
Say each family name and show its regular partner.
lessons.check: Review all five final letter shapes and place each at a word’s end.
lessons.question: Where are final forms placed?
options: At the end of a word
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Review all five final letter shapes and place each at a word’s end.

lessons.title: Chet: A Strong New Sound
lessons.goal: Recognize Chet as a distinct letter and learn its pronunciation from the teacher.
teach: Chet is a different letter from Hey.
Ask the teacher to model the community sound. Learners may listen and echo without forcing the throat.
practice: Find ח among Hey and other shapes.
Listen to the teacher’s pronunciation and echo at a comfortable level.
lessons.check: Recognize Chet as a distinct letter and learn its pronunciation from the teacher.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Chet: A Strong New Sound”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Chet as a distinct letter and learn its pronunciation from the teacher.

lessons.title: Tet and Tav: Similar Sounds, Different Letters
lessons.goal: Recognize Tet and Tav as different letters, even when both represent t.
teach: Tet and Tav have different shapes.
Some traditions pronounce both with t. Point to the letter to identify it, not just the sound.
practice: Find ט and ת in a mixed row.
Name the shape before saying a sound; both may use t in the class tradition.
lessons.check: Recognize Tet and Tav as different letters, even when both represent t.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Tet and Tav: Similar Sounds, Different Letters”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Tet and Tav as different letters, even when both represent t.

lessons.title: The OOOH Vowel Pair: Kubutz and Vav-Shuruk
lessons.goal: Kubutz is the three-dot staircase “OOOH belly”; Vav with its middle dot (Shuruk) also says oo.
teach: Kubutz uses three small dots in a staircase and cues the “OOOH belly.”
Shuruk is Vav with a dot in its middle—the “ball hit the Vav.” Both patterns cue oo.
practice: Count the three Kubutz dots in בֻ and trace their staircase.
Point to the dot inside וּ in בוּ; compare the two oo patterns.
lessons.check: Kubutz is the three-dot staircase “OOOH belly”; Vav with its middle dot (Shuruk) also says oo.
lessons.question: Which two patterns cue oo?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Kubutz is the three-dot staircase “OOOH belly”; Vav with its middle dot (Shuruk) also says oo.

lessons.title: Qof: The Letter Below the Line
lessons.goal: Recognize Qof by its descending shape and learn its class pronunciation.
teach: Recognize Qof by its descending shape and learn its class pronunciation.
Compare ק with כ. Notice Qof’s stroke below the line; then repeat the teacher’s sound model.
practice: Trace ק and point to its descending feature.
Compare Qof with Kaf and say which one drops below.
lessons.check: Recognize Qof by its descending shape and learn its class pronunciation.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Qof: The Letter Below the Line”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Qof by its descending shape and learn its class pronunciation.

lessons.title: Samekh and Zayin: Visual Precision
lessons.goal: Compare the rounded shape of Samekh with the angled shape of Zayin.
teach: Compare the rounded shape of Samekh with the angled shape of Zayin.
Trace ס as a rounded shape and ז as an angled shape. Name each before mixing the cards.
practice: Sort rounded ס and angled ז.
Find each shape in a mixed row and name it.
lessons.check: Compare the rounded shape of Samekh with the angled shape of Zayin.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Samekh and Zayin: Visual Precision”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Compare the rounded shape of Samekh with the angled shape of Zayin.

lessons.title: Gimel: Returning to a Distinct Shape
lessons.goal: Recognize Gimel by its distinct shape and modeled g sound.
teach: Recognize Gimel by its distinct shape and modeled g sound.
Compare ג with ד and ז. Point to Gimel’s distinctive shape, then echo its modeled sound.
practice: Find ג among similar letters.
Trace Gimel and say its class-model sound.
lessons.check: Recognize Gimel by its distinct shape and modeled g sound.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Gimel: Returning to a Distinct Shape”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Recognize Gimel by its distinct shape and modeled g sound.

lessons.title: Review by Family: Quiet, Dotted, Final
lessons.goal: Sort carrier, dotted, and final-form families.
teach: Sort carrier, dotted, and final-form families.
Sort the examples by what to notice: carrier, inside dot, or ending shape. Explain one choice.
examples: א ע · בּ ב · מ ם
practice: Sort א/ע, בּ/ב, and מ/ם into the named families.
Explain one clue used in every group.
lessons.check: Sort carrier, dotted, and final-form families.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Review by Family: Quiet, Dotted, Final”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Sort carrier, dotted, and final-form families.

lessons.title: Review by Shape: Tall, Small, Closed, Confusing
lessons.focus: ל י ח ה ד ר
lessons.goal: Use tall, small, open, closed, and corner features to identify letters.
teach: Use tall, small, open, closed, and corner features to identify letters.
Make three groups from the examples: tall, small, and corner shapes. Move a letter if a partner gives a better visual reason.
examples: ל י · ח ה · ד ר
practice: Sort letters by tall, small, open, closed, and corner features.
Name the specific letter after pointing to its shape clue.
lessons.check: Use tall, small, open, closed, and corner features to identify letters.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Review by Shape: Tall, Small, Closed, Confusing”?
options: ל י ח ה ד ר
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Use tall, small, open, closed, and corner features to identify letters.

lessons.title: Simple Word: Or — Light
lessons.goal: Decode אוֹר and connect it to light; Vav-Cholam was taught earlier.
teach: Point to each letter and mark in אוֹר; read from the right.
Connect the decoded word to light after reading. The Vav-Cholam dot was taught in lesson 13.
practice: Cover the gloss and picture; decode אוֹר.
Uncover the meaning and explain which mark cues oh.
lessons.check: Decode אוֹר and connect it to light; Vav-Cholam was taught earlier.
lessons.question: What does אוֹר mean?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Decode אוֹר and connect it to light; Vav-Cholam was taught earlier.

lessons.title: Simple Word: Shalom
lessons.goal: Decode שָׁלוֹם and connect it to hello or peace.
teach: Point to each letter and mark in שָׁלוֹם.
Decode before using the familiar greeting meaning. The Shin dot and Cholam have already been introduced.
practice: Decode שָׁלוֹם before saying its meaning.
Use it as hello or peace in a teacher-modeled example.
lessons.check: Decode שָׁלוֹם and connect it to hello or peace.
lessons.question: Which word can be a greeting?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Decode שָׁלוֹם and connect it to hello or peace.

lessons.title: Simple Word: Bayit
lessons.goal: Decode בַּיִת and connect it to house.
teach: Point to each part of בַּיִת and follow its known marks.
Read the word first, then connect it to a house. Yod and the Pea Vowel are already familiar.
practice: Read בַּיִת without a picture.
Tell which familiar vowel mark helps with the second beat.
lessons.check: Decode בַּיִת and connect it to house.
lessons.question: What does בַּיִת mean?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Decode בַּיִת and connect it to house.

lessons.title: Names and Hebrew Letters
lessons.goal: Read Hebrew names from their letters and taught vowel marks.
teach: Look at each Hebrew name as Hebrew, from right to left.
Point to the letters and already learned marks; use teacher pronunciation as a model, not English spelling as a shortcut.
practice: Read דָּוִד and מֹשֶׁה from the Hebrew letters.
Point to a vowel mark already studied before saying each name.
lessons.check: Read Hebrew names from their letters and taught vowel marks.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Names and Hebrew Letters”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Read Hebrew names from their letters and taught vowel marks.

lessons.title: Aleph Track Readiness Review
lessons.goal: Show recognition of letters, marks, and familiar words without picture guessing.
teach: Show recognition of letters, marks, and familiar words without picture guessing.
Mix letter and word cards. Identify the letters and marks first; read only patterns already taught.
practice: Name one letter family, one vowel pattern, and one short word.
Read a short example aloud and explain the steps, not just the meaning.
lessons.check: Show recognition of letters, marks, and familiar words without picture guessing.
lessons.question: Which Hebrew form or cue did we practice in “Aleph Track Readiness Review”?
lessons.teacher_note: Model a consistent community pronunciation, respect established differences, and use class cues as memory aids rather than formal definitions.
lessons.feedback: Correct. Show recognition of letters, marks, and familiar words without picture guessing.

lessons.title: Celebration of Beginning
lessons.focus: א ב ג ד ה ו
lessons.goal: Reflect on growth and choose a comfortable next learning step.
